chapter: Returning to the US and the Savoy band
title: Repertoire, radio remotes and pirate air checks
summary: He wrote most of the book, did Saturday-night remote broadcasts, and regrets musicians were not paid for pirated air checks.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Right. And you did all the arrangements, or practically all of them?

I did practically all of them. We had other things in the book ... oh, a couple of things by Andy Gibson, a couple of things by Freddie Norman, and who else did anything? And a couple of things, you know, that the publishers had made up for us when they wanted us to do a radio shot for them, which we did many times -- without any payola.
Yeah.
But I was just thinking of maybe some tunes that were popular as of the moment, and had the audience appeal, you know.
That was these radio spots -- what were they? Late on Saturday night, the radio spots?

Well, I guess they were Saturday nights. You know, they called them Transcontinental broadcasts, you know, remotes, as they called them in those days. They emanated from such places as Frank Dailey's Meadowbrook and all of those ... I think that was the name of it, wasn't it?
Yes.
And other places, you know.
Some of these have been put out, I guess, on pirate records ...
Unfortunately, yes.
These were transcriptions taken from radio broadcasts.
That's right. Which they called 'air checks'.
Air checks. Now I found my way in to records.
Yep.
Well, we're glad that they did; we're sorry that you weren't paid.
Well, I think that people should be paid for their work.
Of course.
It's too bad that the musicians had to suffer because of these things.

This is such an uncontrollable industry, you know, with sound floating through and people with private recording equipment and it's such a difficult thing to track down, and it costs so much money, I guess, to go after pirate editions, that it may be hardly worth it.
Well, that's what I've been told.
